background.definition: Metatarsalgia is a descriptive term used for pain in the forefoot caused by one or more underlying conditions. Primary metatarsalgia refers to conditions of the foot that cause the pain, and secondary metatarsalgia is used when underlying systemic problems are the cause of the pain. Morton's neuroma as a cause of foot pain is discussed in detail in another chapter.

list.listitem: In the United Kingdom, the age-adjusted annual incidence of metatarsalgia is about 50 per 100,000 in men and 88 per 100,000 in women.
summarizes common causes of primary and secondary metatarsalgia.
Repetitive pressure loading under the metatarsal head that exceeds the focal tissue tolerance leads to inflammation and pain.
Disequilibrium in biomechanics leads to abnormal weight distribution among the metatarsal heads causing increased pressure under the metatarsal heads.

The plantar plate is a fibrocartilage structure residing on the inferior surfaces of the lesser metatarsophalangeal joints. Plantar plate injury or tears can result from overloading the metatarsophalangeal joint; this can result in joint instability, pain, swelling and toe dislocation with crossover deformities.

Nonmechanical damage can occur with systemic diseases to the anatomical structures including bone, cartilage, capsule, ligaments, blood vessels, lymph vessels, nerves, tendons, bursae, SC tissue, and skin.
Careful clinical evaluation is the most accurate way to make the appropriate diagnosis. B
Mulder's test is sensitive and specific in the diagnosis of Morton's neuroma. B
MRI and ultrasound are sensitive and highly specific in evaluating patients with metatarsalgia of various etiologies, especially when symptoms persist for more than 6 to 12 weeks. B
The typical symptom is pain along the plantar aspect of the metatarsal heads.
The complaint of burning pain and numbness, especially in the interspace between the third and fourth metatarsals, is often related to Morton's neuroma.
Among patients with surgically confirmed neuromas, 96% report symptoms that are worse with activity, 84% report improvement with rest, 76% feel worse while in shoes, and 68% report paresthesias.

Among consecutive patients referred for imaging to evaluate metatarsalgia, about one-third have symptoms of Morton's neuroma. However, about one-third of patients found to have neuromas on MRI have no symptoms.

In a retrospective study of 90 patients who underwent surgical repair for plantar plate tears, nearly all patients (95%) presented with gradual onset of forefoot pain, edema, and a positive drawer sign. High specificity (greater than 80%) was found for a positive drawer test (99.8%) and crossover toes (88.9%).

To perform Mulder's test for Morton's neuroma, apply pressure to the interdigital space. A positive test occurs when the patient experiences a "click" and nerve-irritating symptoms into the involved toes. This is present in 84% to 95% of patients with surgically confirmed neuromas. In addition, its specificity approaches 100%.

The dorsal plantar drawer test is performed to detect MTP joint stability. The involved toe is dorsiflexed 25° at the MTP joint and the toe (usually the second toe) is grasped between the thumb and index finger and the MTP joint is stressed in a vertical direction. Instability of the joint is demonstrated by increased upward mobility at the joint
The initial imaging study, plain x-ray of the foot, is often normal, especially with early symptoms and in patients with no acute trauma.
In detecting Morton's neuroma and other causes of metatarsalgia, the sensitivity of MRI is about 85% (64%-95%) but specificity approaches 100%.

In a case series of 85 patients with metatarsalgia undergoing MRI, a normal plantar plate was demonstrated in 75 feet, followed by degenerative plantar lesions in 25 feet, and complete plantar plate rupture in 5 feet.
Ultrasound (US) for interdigital soft tissue lesions is comparable to MRI and is 79% sensitive (59%-91%) and nearly 100% specific (55%-100%), especially if the lesion size is above 6 mm.

Authors of a meta-analysis showed that the sensitivity of US (91%) was equal to that of MRI (90%) for the identification of Morton's neuroma, suggesting that US may be the most cost-effective imaging method for this condition.
If there is clinical suspicion of neurologic, vascular, or systemic etiology, proceed with EMG and nerve conduction study, ankle brachial index/ratio, and/or limited laboratory testing.
If a digital nerve block just below the transverse ligament leads to pain relief, this supports the diagnosis of Morton's neuroma/nerve entrapment.
In-shoe dynamic pressure-measuring systems and plantar pressure and force-measuring systems can identify areas of abnormal weight distribution pressure abnormalities.
summarizes a suggested approach to managing the patient with metatarsalgia.
Consider referral for the patient who fails to respond after 6 to 12 weeks of conservative treatment.
Begin treating patients with ice, rest, activity adjustments to reduce metatarsal pressure, and simple analgesics such as NSAID or acetaminophen. C
Metatarsal pads and custom-made or semirigid orthotics reduce pain, including pain in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. B
Compared to metatarsal pads, the metatarsal bars in an oblique position had the greatest reduction of impulse on the second metatarsal head in healthy subjects. B

Injection therapy with steroids or alcohol can be considered. Neurolysis or neurectomy appear to result in greater incidences of complete pain relief and patient satisfaction outcomes compared to injection treatment. Overall, there is insufficient evidence with which to assess the effectiveness of surgical interventions for Morton's neuroma. B
If there is no resolution or significant improvement of the pain and symptoms within 6 to 12 weeks, consider referral to an orthopedic foot surgeon or podiatrist. C
For patients with plantar plate tears, plantar plate repair can be performed and appears to improve pain and function. B
Initiate treatment with simple analgesics such as NSAID or acetaminophen.

Iontophoresis with ketorolac or with placebo provides similar immediate relief in patients with pain from rheumatic disease. However, after 7 days, patients receiving ketorolac had significant reductions in pain scores, whereas those receiving placebo did not.

In patients with interdigital neuralgia/Morton's neuroma, at the end of 9 months, 28% treated with ultrasound-guided steroid injection had complete pain relief, whereas 31% had little or no relief. In an evaluator-blinded randomized trial of 56 patients with Morton's neuroma, ultrasound-guided steroid injection provided greater symptomatic relief over blind injection at 45 days, 2 months and 3 months.

In patients with Morton's neuroma, at the end of 6 months, 84% of those treated with ultrasound-guided alcohol injection were pain free. A second case series with 85 subjects found similar results with partial or total treatment response achieved in 66%. Twenty percent required surgery due to continued pain.

Authors of a meta-analysis including 35 papers reporting on 2998 individuals with Morton's neuroma, found injection therapy performed less well than neurolysis or neurectomy for complete pain relief and patient satisfaction; the incidence of complete pain relief with injection therapy was 43%, 95% CI 23-64% which was significantly lower than neurolysis (68%, 95% CI 51-84%) and neurectomy (74%, 95% CI 66-82%).

Surgical measures should be considered after failure of nonsurgical treatment, impracticality of nonsurgical treatment, or if the patient desires surgical resolution of a deformity causing pain and loss of function.

Metatarsal osteotomies, performed for metatarsalgia, can be proximal or distal. The former does not violate the joint but results in a high rate of nonunion when done without internal fixation. The latter procedures are associated with an increased incidence of recurrent metatarsalgia, joint stiffness, and floating toe.
Overall, there is insufficient evidence with which to assess the effectiveness of surgical interventions for Morton's neuroma.

For patients with plantar plate tears, plantar plate repair can be performed. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies involving 537 plantar plate tears who underwent repairs using either a dorsal or plantar approach found improvements in both pain (pooled mean change of -5.01 [95%CI -5.36, -4.66] pre-to postoperative on a visual analog scale) and function (improvement in American Orthopedic Foot and Ankle Society scores of 40.44 [95%CI 37.90, 42.97]).
Magnetic insoles were no more effective than sham insoles in alleviating chronic nonspecific foot pain in the workplace.
Manipulative Therapy (MT) could be considered for short-term treatment of metatarsalgia.
Conservative measures include ice, rest, and activity adjustments to reduce metatarsal pressure.
Patients with significant callus in weight-bearing areas may benefit from callous debridement by the patient with a pumice stone.
Metatarsal pads redistribute pressure more evenly and decrease pain scores.

In patients with nonspecific metatarsalgia, custom-molded orthotics or a rocker bar resulted in greater pain relief than ready-made insoles. The addition of a rocker bar to a custom-made orthotic did not provide additional relief.

In an RCT with 72 patients with Morton's neuroma, patients randomized to use of a customized insole with metatarsal and arch support had less pain with walking and better physical activity and function compared to a control group who received a flat insole of the same material, color, and density.
Using an adjustable toe splint can decrease metatarsalgia in patients with lesser toe deformity, but can cause toe abrasions.
In patients with rheumatoid arthritis, the use of semirigid orthotics caused significant reductions in pain, but supportive shoes or soft orthotics provided no relief.
If there is no resolution or significant improvement of the pain and symptoms within 6 to 12 weeks, consider referral to an orthopedic foot surgeon or podiatrist.
Among patients with Morton's neuroma treated surgically, long-term follow-up reveals that about one-half had good or excellent outcomes and 40% had poor outcomes. B
Patient reported satisfaction after resection of a Morton's neuroma in a recent case series was similar with 10/99 reporting poor or very poor results; only 63% were pain-free at 6-month follow up.
Patients with lesions in the second web space had worse outcomes. B
Generalized atrophy of fat tissue in the elderly may affect the metatarsal fad pads and increase the risk of developing metatarsalgia.
Secondary causes may be more common in the elderly, as systemic illness is more common in this age group.

cell.label: Forefoot pain under the metatarsal heads. Specific cause suggested by exam?
cell.path: Point bone tenderness, swelling, recent increase in activity
Burning or numbness between the toes, positive Mulder sign
Second toe joint swelling or drifting toe
Bunion, claw or hammer toes, or high arch

cell.label: Conservative care for 6–12 weeks: wide toe box, metatarsal pad or insole, weight loss, activity change, NSAIDs

Weight-bearing X-ray if not done; check for systemic causes: diabetes or neuropathy (glucose, monofilament), peripheral artery disease (ankle–brachial index), inflammatory arthritis (ESR, CRP), gout (uric acid)
Possible stress fracture. X-ray (often normal early; MRI if needed). Protected weight bearing.
Probable Morton neuroma. Wide shoes, metatarsal pad; ultrasound if unclear.
Plantar plate injury or MTP joint synovitis. Taping, stiff-soled shoe; refer if persistent.
Gout or infection. Aspirate and send for cells, culture, crystals.
Ultrasound or MRI; podiatry or orthopedic referral.

footnotes.footnote: Check sensation and pulses in every patient with diabetes.

feature.caption: Causes of Metatarsalgia.
feature.feature_body:
Primary Secondary
High-impact sports Excess weight from pregnancy or obesity
Excessive standing or walking Rheumatoid arthritis
Wearing high-heeled shoes with small toe box or other ill-fitting shoes Ankylosing spondylitis
Narrow feet with very high arches Diabetes mellitus
Tight Achilles tendon Gout
Morton's neuroma Peripheral artery disease
Morton's foot/toe (short first toe) Lyme disease
Pes cavus, pes planus Osteomyelitis
Hallux valgus and claw/hammer toe Peripheral nerve compression
Callus
Fat pad atrophy
Sesamoiditis
Stress fracture
Osteonecrosis or avascular necrosis (Freiberg's disease)
Data from Bardelli M, Turelli L, Scoccianti G. Definition and classification of metatarsalgia. Foot Ankle Surg 2003;9:79-85.
